pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (identical to the printed 'n of 15' pagination)

entry.evidence: no study, to our knowledge, has investigated how different ice thickness thresholds

steps.action: The authors pose the gap: how will the duration of ice above activity-specific safety thickness thresholds change under warming across the Northern Hemisphere?
steps.quote: no study, to our knowledge, has investigated how different ice thickness thresholds

steps.action: The authors rely on earlier evaluations of the LISSS 1-D lake model against observations as the premise for its use.
steps.quote: LISSS has been shown to provide an accurate representation of water temperature, surface fluxes, and the thickness of ice and snow

steps.action: The authors use the CESM2 large ensemble (historical 1850-2014 plus SSP3-7.0), 90 members with daily LISSS lake ice thickness on a 1-degree grid; the ensemble was run in the co-authors' earlier work (Rodgers et al., 2021).
steps.quote: Daily simulations of 4,622 lake grids in 90 members spanning 251 years yielded >30 billion total data points

steps.action: The authors define safe-ice days as days with thickness of at least 10 cm (recreation) and 13, 30.5 and 107 cm (transport), each held for at least 7 days; they set global-warming levels with 15-year windows and a 1900-1929 baseline.
steps.quote: number of days that the projected ice thickness is equal or greater than 10 cm

steps.action: The authors import 2020 gridded population density (GPWv4) and a 1901-2010 Köppen climate classification, regridded to the model grid for stratification.
steps.quote: population data for 2020 were extracted from the Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center

steps.action: The authors compute the historical safe-ice duration (152 days on average) and its projected loss (13, 17 and 24 days at 1.5, 2 and 3 degrees C; about 7.7 days per degree C) from the ensemble mean.
steps.quote: the duration of safe lake ice will shorten, on average, by 13 days

steps.action: The authors analyse each ensemble member independently and show the member spread around the mean (Figure 1b; standard deviation in Figure 2c) to separate the forced signal from internal variability.
steps.quote: Here, we analyzed individual ensemble members independently and then calculated ensemble averages.

steps.action: The authors compare projected losses across latitude bands and Köppen zones: the largest absolute losses are in cold, northern regions and the largest percent losses at lower latitudes and in the Mild temperate zone.
steps.quote: the absolute change in the duration of safe lake ice will be greatest in the coldest regions, including the northernmost latitudes

steps.action: The authors set the percent loss of safe ice against population density and find the largest percent losses in the most densely populated grids.
steps.quote: the percent change in the duration of safe ice under future warming will be greatest in the most densely populated regions

steps.action: The authors compute historical and projected safe-ice durations for the snowmobile, car/pickup and transport-truck thresholds (Figures 5-7, Table 1).
steps.quote: The number of days with safe lake ice for transport trucks is projected to decrease by 90%, 95%, and 99%

steps.action: The authors compare losses across thickness thresholds and find that the relative loss grows with the required thickness.
steps.quote: will differ depending on the ice thickness requirements

steps.action: The authors set the projected loss against the cited expectation that air temperature dominates lake ice thickness, and explain it by a shorter ice-growth season.
steps.quote: Intuitively, our simulations suggest that the duration of safe lake ice will shorten across the Northern Hemisphere

steps.action: The authors qualify the 10 cm black-ice threshold: more white ice in warm, wet winters would demand thicker ice, so the safety criterion is likely optimistic.
steps.quote: ice will need to be even greater than 10 cm thick to be safer for people to use

steps.action: The authors retain the projections as robust large-scale patterns and list caveats: typical-lake aggregation, 1-D physics, snow uncertainty, no human snow clearing, uniform thresholds and a black-ice assumption.
steps.quote: Although we consider our results robust and believe that they bridge an important knowledge-gap, there are several caveats

tree.answer: Lake ice loss under warming, established in prior literature
No; future safe-ice duration is not observable and is obtained by simulation
Estimate changes in safe-ice duration by threshold, warming level and region
Conditions set in the model: historical plus SSP3-7.0 forcing, warming levels of 1.5, 2 and 3 degrees C
Signal stands out against spread across 90 initial-condition ensemble members; no observational or multi-model check
Projections kept as estimates with ensemble spread, with caveats

end.claim: Safe lake ice for recreation across the Northern Hemisphere shortens on average by 13, 17 and 24 days at 1.5, 2 and 3 degrees C of warming, and safe-ice days for heavy transport trucks decline by 90%, 95% and 99%.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the 90-member CESM2-LE runs giving daily prognostic lake ice thickness, which the safety thresholds are applied to, no projection of safe-ice duration would exist.

gates.evidence: No hypothesis directed data acquisition: an existing ensemble was mined. The projected safe-ice durations are not tested against observed ice thickness or other models, only set against ensemble spread. Thresholds come from external safety guidance (Minnesota DNR; Block et al., 2019), but nothing says they were fixed before the output was examined.

imports.item: Gridded Population of the World v4 population density (2020)
Ice thickness safety thresholds for people, snowmobiles, cars and trucks (Minnesota Department of Natural Resources)
Köppen climate classification, built on the empirical climate-vegetation relation

novelty_claims.quote: In this study, we provide the first quantitative assessment of changes in the duration of safe lake ice for recreation
no study, to our knowledge, has investigated how different ice thickness thresholds

limits:
Single published paper; no review file, so no review sequence.

The ensemble simulations were run in the co-authors' earlier work (Rodgers et al., 2021) and are coded as inherited. Model skill for lake ice thickness rests on cited validation (Subin et al., 2012); no comparison with observed ice thickness or safe-ice records is made here.

Only one model and one scenario (SSP3-7.0) are used; there is no multi-model or threshold-sensitivity test.

The V check is the spread across initial-condition members, coded as robustness. Inference: it could also be read as reproduction (a rerun of a stochastic model under the same forcing), which would make V partial.

Composition is none_fits: this is a projection study, not a forecast frozen and later verified, and no rivals are posed.

Sub-claims, all at estimate_with_resolution: latitudinal and Köppen-zone contrasts, the largest percent loss in densely populated grids, and threshold-dependent losses for transport. These are reported mostly without significance tests.

Some reported numbers carry sign inconsistencies, for example Mild temperate '80.1 ± 20.5%' and Table 1 Polar 2 degrees C '(12)'. The text gives inconsistent latitude bands for the 17/24/35-day losses (north of 45°N on p. 4, >60°N on p. 11).

disagreements.target: Recent lake ice studies using ice duration as a proxy for winter ecosystem services (e.g., Brammer et al., 2015)
disagreements.support: The authors argue that duration alone is insufficient and that thickness thresholds must be modelled, which they then do.
disagreements.quote: accurately projecting how these ecosystem services might change within a warming world requires a consideration of changes in lake ice thickness

disagreements.target: Arp et al. (2019), on increased freshwater supply for Alaskan ice roads
disagreements.support: Their projected loss of ice thicker than 107 cm implies that more water supply may not keep ice roads viable for heavy loads.
disagreements.quote: the ice may not be sufficiently thick to sustain the heavy loads carried by transport trucks

alternatives_considered.reason: deemed suitably early to provide a benchmark against any signature of anthropogenic warming

alternatives_considered.chosen: 10 cm threshold assuming strongest black ice
alternatives_considered.reason: minimal ice thickness required to sustain human weight

alternatives_considered.chosen: Large ensemble, members analysed individually then averaged
alternatives_considered.reason: to deconvolve the forced signal from natural variability

alternatives_considered.chosen: Aggregated typical lake per 1-degree grid cell with 1-D physics
alternatives_considered.alternatives: individual lakes; resolving horizontal intra-lake structure
alternatives_considered.reason: not possible to resolve individual lakes at CMIP6 resolution

alternatives_considered.chosen: Uniform ice thickness/duration requirements across the region
alternatives_considered.alternatives: road-specific thickness requirements; snow clearing on ice roads
alternatives_considered.reason: allowed us to isolate the climate change impact on the presence of safe ice
